cim: What’s next for data centers as Texas prepares for political shift?
cim_eredeti: What’s next for data centers as Texas prepares for political shift?
szoveg_eredeti:
(NewsNation) — Texas is emerging as a major test for the future of AI data center development after voters elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa governor, ending 36 years of Republican leadership in the state.

Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott Tuesday, making history as Texas’ first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor elected since Ann Richards in 1990.

A major issue behind her campaign was the rapid expansion of AI data centers and the pressure that development could put on local communities.

Texas accounts for roughly one-quarter of planned U.S. data center capacity, putting the state at the center of the nation’s AI infrastructure boom.

Hinojosa has called for keeping new data center approvals paused until lawmakers establish stronger protections. Her priorities include safeguarding water supplies, preventing residents from shouldering higher electricity costs and giving local communities more transparency and input over proposed projects.

Abbott had already halted certain state permits and grid connections while ordering a data center audit. Hinojosa, however, is seeking long-term safeguards.

She takes office Jan. 19, 2027, and will need lawmakers to pass new legislation to put those protections in place.

Texas isn’t alone in facing growing resistance to large-scale data center projects.

Democrats who campaigned on tighter restrictions also won gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio, raising questions about whether the election results could signal a broader shift in how states approach AI infrastructure.

According to Politico and industry tracker Cleanview, 41% of the nation’s planned data center pipeline is in states with existing or proposed moratoriums.

Local voters also backed limits on developments. Ballotpedia reports that as of Wednesday, 46 of 47 decided local data center measures in 2026 favored greater restrictions. Those results include measures decided before Election Day.

The proposed restrictions vary, ranging from temporary construction pauses to stricter zoning requirements, additional oversight and limits on new development.

Critics argue the rapid expansion could strain electricity grids and water resources while raising costs for communities.

Meanwhile, industry advocates warn delays could discourage investment and slow economic growth.

Growing political pushback is pressuring technology companies to address concerns from communities where they plan to build.

OpenAI announced commitments to cover electricity and related infrastructure costs, develop water plans and give communities greater input at future campuses it owns and operates.

Separately, NewsNation partner The Hill reports major technology companies and environmental groups are negotiating a possible national framework for responsible data center development. No final agreement has been announced.

The challenge for Hinojosa and other newly elected governors is balancing economic growth with protections for their communities.

Texas, as one of the biggest markets for AI development, could become a major test of how that balance works.
